claims.text: Catalytic activity in nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs ethanol-oxidation catalysts is governed by the surface electronic structure.
The degree of surface Pt enrichment shifts the catalyst d-band center.
The d-band-center shift modulates adsorption energies of ethanol and its reaction intermediates.
Changes in adsorption energies caused by the d-band shift tune ethanol-oxidation kinetics.
The initial nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs catalysts are uniform high-entropy solid solutions.
The initial catalyst surfaces have statistically random distributions of the constituent elements.
Controlled electrochemical potential cycling can selectively drive Pt surface segregation in PtPdRhRuIrOs nanoparticles.
The proposed potential cycling can induce Pt surface segregation without altering the bulk catalyst structure.
Pt-enriched near-surface active sites alter the local electronic environment.
Potential-cycling-induced Pt segregation shifts the d-band center downward.
A downward d-band-center shift reduces the binding energy of ethanol-oxidation intermediates to an optimal level.
Optimized intermediate binding balances adsorption and reaction steps and thereby enhances catalytic turnover.
Relative to an untreated catalyst, the treated catalyst will show increased cyclic-voltammetry current density and a more favorable ethanol-oxidation onset potential.
The untreated baseline has a homogeneous surface distribution of all constituent elements.
The proposed mechanism is expected to hold at room temperature in acidic aqueous ethanol electrolyte for similarly nanostructured particles, typically smaller than 10 nm.
The proposed mechanism may not hold at high temperature or substantially different pH because other degradation processes can dominate.

contradictions.description: PtPdRhRuIrOs contains six named elements, whereas the material-initial-state and baseline fields refer to a distribution of all seven elements.
